title: Kaddish is praise
hookLine: an Aramaic prayer praising God, said by mourners, that never mentions death

cards: In films and novels, the Kaddish usually turns up in one scene: the graveside, a son or daughter standing, a few murmured Aramaic words. It gets called the Jewish prayer for the dead. And mourners do say it.
But read the words of the mourner's version, and something strange happens. There is no death in it. No grave, no loss, no person who has died, no afterlife.
It doesn't even mention the mourner. It praises God, line after line, and closes by asking for peace.

teach.b: Kaddish means holy, or sanctification. It's in Aramaic, the everyday language many Jews spoke in the time of the Talmud, not Hebrew.

Its first words are yitgadal v'yitkadash shmeh rabba: magnified and sanctified be His great name. Those two verbs echo Ezekiel, in the old Jewish translation: "Thus will I magnify Myself, and sanctify Myself."
Then it asks that God's kingship be established in our lives and our days, soon.

teach.h: THE ROOM ANSWERS: MAY HIS NAME BE BLESSED.
teach.b: At the center comes the line the whole congregation answers aloud: y'hei shmeh rabba, may His great name be blessed forever and ever. The Talmud treats that answer as huge.
In tractate Shabbat, a teacher says whoever answers it with all their strength has a harsh decree against them torn up.

Kaddish likely began not in mourning but in the study house: after a teacher finished a lesson, everyone praised God together. That version is still said after learning. In the service it comes in several forms.
A short one marks the joints between sections, like a bookmark. A full one closes the main prayer. One follows study.
And one is said by mourners.
So when a mourner stands up, they aren't saying a prayer about death. They're leading the room in praise, at the very moment praise is hardest. Tomorrow, why they do it.

how: Kaddish is said only with a minyan: the leader or the mourners recite it, and the congregation answers amen and the line y'hei shmeh rabba aloud. Different forms of it mark the sections of the service, close the Amidah, follow study, and are said by mourners.

games.q: you're in the congregation. the leader says: magnified and sanctified be his great name. a moment later the leader pauses. what do you do?
o: stay silent; it's the leader's prayer.
answer aloud: amen, may his great name be blessed forever.
games.why: the congregation answers aloud. the Talmud praises answering y'hei shmeh rabba with all your strength.

practice: Bring back a word of praise you heard lately, a friend saying the sunset was beautiful, a child proud of a drawing, a grandparent thanking God for a meal, and hear it again.
Then answer it quietly, amen, yes, so be it, because in the Kaddish the answering is half the prayer.
